purpose: Olutasidenib is used to treat a type of blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in adults whose cancer has a specific gene mutation called IDH1. It is used when the leukemia has come back or has not responded to other treatments. Your doctor will test your cancer cells to make sure this drug is the right fit for you.
how_it_works: In some people with AML, a faulty IDH1 gene causes cancer cells to grow out of control. Olutasidenib works like a key that blocks this faulty gene, slowing down or stopping the cancer cells from growing. By targeting this specific mutation, it helps your body's blood cells mature more normally again.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, tiredness, joint or muscle pain, constipation, diarrhea, shortness of breath, low red blood cell counts (anemia), increased liver enzyme levels, and swelling in the arms or legs. Some people also experience rash or fever.
warnings: A serious condition called differentiation syndrome can occur, which may cause fever, trouble breathing, fluid buildup, or low blood pressure — seek medical help right away if these happen. This drug can cause liver problems, so your doctor will monitor your liver with blood tests. It may harm an unborn baby, so use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 30 days after. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, as this drug can interact with many others.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 150 mg taken by mouth twice a day, approximately every 12 hours. It can be taken with or without food. Try to take it at the same times each day, and swallow the capsules whole — do not open or crush them.
